_help: Tone of what was actually SAID: -2 strongly leaning toward rate cuts .. 0 neutral .. +2 strongly leaning toward rate hikes, for the currency's own central bank. Use plain wording in these notes ("leaning toward higher rates / rate cuts"), not hawkish/dovish. Keys come from data/speakers.json (field 'key'). Only central-bank speakers feed the CB-stance checklist indicator; treasury/finance-ministry entries are scored for the record but excluded from stance. Unscored events stay pending and contribute nothing.
_note_AUD_minutes: RBA held 4.35% on 11 Aug. Minutes said inflation remains too high and the board could raise the cash rate again if upside risks materialise - held rates but leaning toward a hike. Next decision 29 Sep 2026.
_note_USD_barkin: Mixed, not a clear signal. Called it an 'open question' whether a hike is needed and gave reasons price pressures may ease on their own, but warned above-target inflation since 2021 risks becoming 'more embedded'. The 26 Aug appearance was on rising US debt leading to an eventual 'reckoning' - fiscal, not policy-path, so scored flat.
_note_USD_bessent: NOT monetary policy - a new round of Iran sanctions ('Operation Economic Outcast'), including removing entities from the US dollar system. Geopolitically material and dollar-relevant, but says nothing about the rate path, so scored flat and excluded from CB stance by the non-central-bank rule.
_note_USD_fomc_minutes_jul: Clearly leaning toward higher rates. 9-3 hold with THREE regional presidents voting for a 25bp hike (Hammack/Cleveland, Kashkari/Minneapolis, Logan/Dallas). The group wanting higher rates was wider than the dissent: 'Several participants favored an increase of 25 basis points at this meeting' and 'many participants assessed that policy tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline'. Some said rates may not be high enough to slow the economy. Schmid and Musalem, non-voters in July, said they would have backed a hike. Not +2 because the committee still held and a September hike was described as far from set. NOTE: the dollar FELL ~0.7% on the day despite the higher-rates message.
_note_USD_warsh: Leaning toward higher rates. In his first Jackson Hole keynote as Chair, Warsh called inflation 'concerning' and said the summer readings 'do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved' and that the Fed has 'work to do', suggesting rates 'may have to' rise in the coming months. But he pointedly gave no explicit signal on September and doubled down on providing less forward guidance ('we should not indulge a regime in which market participants are looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade'), so this is +1 not +2. Markets still repriced toward higher rates: CME September hike odds jumped from ~35% to ~46-56% (now a coin flip), the dollar index rallied to a one-week high, front-end yields rose and gold fell ~2.8%.
_note_USD_hammack: Clearly leaning toward higher rates. Cleveland Fed's Hammack - a July dissenter for a 25bp hike - said from Jackson Hole 'I believe now is the time to act' and repeated her call for higher rates, arguing inflation has run above 2% for over five years and rates show no sign of being high enough to slow the economy. An explicit push for a near-term hike.
_note_EUR_lagarde_wef: Not policy-path. Lagarde's WEF panel was on structural/geopolitical themes - Europe's post-war growth model 'eroding', US retreat from a rules-based order, competitiveness - with nothing on the ECB rate trajectory. Scored flat for the record.
_note_EUR_board_misc: Three ECB appearances with no rate-path content: Lane on defence spending and the euro-area economy (fiscal/structural); Cipollone's ilsussidiario.net interview on the Single Market and firm competitiveness, in which he said the ECB has no plans to change its rate trajectory and played down Hormuz stagflation risk (steady/neutral); Schnabel's Jackson Hole paper 'Central banks on-chain' on tokenisation and settlement. All scored flat. NOTE: Schnabel's separate 26 Aug remarks that 'rates must rise more' are a different event, not in the pending list.
_note_USD_jh_day1: Leaning toward higher rates. Opening day (Schmid welcoming remarks + dinner). In same-day media, Kansas City Fed's Schmid called inflation 'still stubborn and still sticky', said the 3.5-3.75% policy rate may be helping growth rather than slowing it, and that a hike could be justified as soon as the 16 Sep meeting; reporting had two-to-three Fed officials issuing inflation warnings on the day. No formal policy set-piece on the 27th itself, hence +1 not +2.
_note_USD_jh_day2: Leaning toward higher rates. Keynote day: Warsh's first Jackson Hole address as Chair - inflation 'running above our 2 percent target', 'we have work to do', explicitly would not rule out a hike and pushed back on rate-cut expectations, though he gave no September signal and rejected mechanical forward guidance. Cleveland's Hammack, same day, said 'now is the time to act' on higher rates. CME September-hike odds moved from ~35% toward a coin flip, DXY hit a one-week high, front-end yields up, gold down ~2-3%. Umbrella score blends the careful keynote with the explicit push for a hike on the day; the speaker-specific entries USD|Fed Chairman Warsh Speaks (+1) and USD|FOMC Member Hammack Speaks (+2) carry the same signal.
_note_USD_jh_day3: Flat. Final half-day was academic paper panels and non-Fed participants (e.g. Austria's Kocher on euro-area momentum); no new Fed policy-path content beyond what Warsh and Schmid had already delivered. Scored 0 to avoid a third count of the same message.
_note_GBP_mann_jh: Flat - not about the BoE policy path. Mann spoke at Jackson Hole on 'Financial Innovation and the International Monetary System', a topical/structural address on external imbalances and cross-border spillovers, not UK rates. Mann is an MPC member known for wanting higher rates and for dissenting, but this speech carried no signal on the Bank Rate trajectory, so scored 0 per the policy-path-only rule.
_note_NZD_rbnz_sep: The 2 Sep MPS delivered a unanimous second straight 25bp hike to 2.75%, citing inflation at 4.1% (fuel-driven; 2.9% ex-fuel) and a majority of the MPC seeing upside risks - the Monetary Policy Statement itself projects a chance of one further hike before year-end, so +2. Gov Breman's press conference kept the hike option 'firmly on the table' and said the RBNZ 'remains resolved to adjust the OCR higher', but framed the next move as more a December discussion, hence +1.5. The following morning (20:10 UTC = 3 Sep NZ) at Parliament's Finance and Expenditure select committee she said that after two hikes the RBNZ 'can probably take some time to assess' how they have affected the economy - a pause hint, softer than the tightening bias but not an easing signal, so -0.5.
_note_CAD_boc_sep: The 2 Sep decision held the overnight rate at 2.25% for a 7th straight meeting. The statement and Macklem's opening remarks leaned on elevated upside inflation risks - CPI hovering near 3% on gasoline, Middle East energy prices, and new US-Canada tariffs after trade talks broke down ('the longer oil prices and refinery margins stay high, the greater the risk that higher energy prices spill over') - against a broadening 3.3% Q2 recovery. But the Bank explicitly gave no signal and stayed data-dependent ('prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed'), so only a mild +0.5 on each.
_note_EUR_nagel_sep: Nagel backed the September ECB hike path (markets >95% priced) and 'strongly signalled' the ECB will raise rates, while welcoming the easing in core and services inflation and saying he sees no second-round effects; he stressed a meeting-by-meeting approach beyond September given volatile energy prices. Clearly leaning toward higher rates but with the good-inflation-news caveat and no commitment past September, so +1.5. The 1 Sep and 2 Sep entries are the same message.
_note_USD_barr_sep: Leaning toward higher rates, two-sided. At the Second Chance Lending Forum Barr said inflation 'remains too high - and has been for over five years' and that if it 'appears not to be moderating sufficiently, then I think we should act decisively to raise rates' at the 15-16 Sep FOMC, while adding that if the data give confidence inflation is on a path to 2% the Fed 'can take a bit more time'. Open to a hike or a hold depending on the data, so +1.
_note_EUR_vujcic_households: Flat - a research/communications speech, not policy-path. ECB VP Vujcic argued that high-quality household expectations surveys support better policymaking and credibility, and that central banks should communicate the uncertainty around the baseline and alternative scenarios (referencing the June 2026 Eurosystem projections). Nothing on the ECB rate trajectory, so scored 0 for the record.
